record.paper_title: Dynamical criticality: overview and open questions
record.original_question: Under what conditions does evolutionary dynamics favor systems in a critical regime rather than ordered or disordered regimes? More specifically, given that a system's task performance is measured by a fitness function that is often related to the attractor landscape defining its dynamic repertoire, for which classes of tasks, fitness landscapes, and environmental dynamics are critical systems preferred by evolution? The open problem is to characterize the task features and landscape parameters, including properties such as correlation lengths, rates of environmental change, and the amount of that change, that determine when critical systems have an evolutionary advantage.

evidence.quote: The identification of the conditions under which evolutionary dynamics favours critical systems is still a fundamental open question.
In particular, this requires the definition of a function that measures the effectiveness with which a system accomplishes a given task, i.e. a fitness function.

We expect, on the basis of reasonable guesses and of previous studies, that critical systems will not always be preferred, since the outcome depends upon tasks features (see [10]). Therefore the goal is indeed quite complicated, as it amounts to finding out for which kind of tasks critical systems are better.

The different types of tasks should therefore be categorized in a proper way, in particular by the value of some parameters that describe the main characteristics of the fitness landscape (e.g. correlation lengths) and of its own dynamics (e.g. the rate of change and its amount).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a family of dynamical systems parametrized by a control parameter $c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that the dynamics admit three qualitatively distinct regimes: an ordered regime ($c < c^*$), a critical regime ($c = c^*$), and a disordered (chaotic) regime ($c > c^*$). For each system, the dynamic repertoire is encoded by an attractor landscape $\mathcal{A}(c)$ (the collection of attractors together with their basins under the deterministic or stochastic update rule).

Let $\mathcal{T}$ denote a class of tasks. A task $T \in \mathcal{T}$ comes equipped with a fitness function
$$F_T : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R},$$
that assigns to each attractor landscape a real-valued performance score quantifying how effectively the system accomplishes $T$. The environment is modeled as a stochastic process $\{E_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ taking values in a space of task instances, characterized by:
(i) a correlation length $\xi$ describing spatial/structural correlations of the fitness landscape over the configuration space,
(ii) a temporal rate of change $r$ at which $E_t$ evolves, and
(iii) an amplitude $\Delta$ measuring the magnitude of environmental variations.

An evolutionary dynamics is a Markov process on the parameter $c$ whose stationary distribution $\pi_{T,\xi,r,\Delta}(c)$ concentrates around values of $c$ that maximize the long-run expected fitness $\mathbb{E}[F_{E_t}(\mathcal{A}(c))]$.

Problem. Determine, as a function of the task class $\mathcal{T}$ and the parameters $(\xi, r, \Delta)$, the set
$$\mathcal{C} := \{ (T,\xi,r,\Delta) : \pi_{T,\xi,r,\Delta} 	ext{ is concentrated at } c = c^* \}.$$
That is, characterize precisely the task features and the landscape/environmental parameters $(\xi, r, \Delta)$ for which evolutionary dynamics select the critical regime over the ordered or disordered regimes, and provide explicit conditions (inequalities or threshold relations) separating the regions of parameter space where ordered, critical, or disordered systems are evolutionarily favored.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of when evolutionary dynamics select critical systems remains an active and unresolved research direction. Subsequent literature on criticality in biological and adaptive systems (e.g., works by Hidalgo, Grigera, Munoz and others on "information-based fitness and the emergence of criticality") provides partial results in specific models, showing criticality can be advantageous in variable environments, but no general characterization in terms of task class and environmental parameters has been established.

status_evidence.title: Information-based fitness and the emergence of criticality in living systems
status_evidence.snippet: Empirical evidence and theoretical arguments suggest that systems performing complex tasks under variable environments operate near criticality.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress exists for specific models showing criticality is favored in variable environments, but a general characterization is not given.

status_evidence.title: Dynamical criticality: overview and open questions
status_evidence.snippet: The identification of the conditions under which evolutionary dynamics favours critical systems is still a fundamental open question.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is stated as open.
